name: Amira Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or technology firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What is a normal shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a haul-truck crew at a large mine and check the tire and hydraulic notes before the first run. Once a month I use an approved assistant to translate a section of the service manual, then I ask the mechanic to confirm the wording before I pass it on.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you value about the job, and what makes it hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I can teach someone a safe route and still trust them to make their own call. The rotating nights are tiring, but I earn high pay and have eleven months of expenses saved, so I can consider a change without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a small tool can sort routine notices, but it should not make the safety decision. I will keep my own route checks in the loop, even if a screen saves time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is mostly hands-on and this picture only automates some routine tasks, so I do not expect my income to change. I have eleven months saved and similar mines nearby, which means I can judge the tool on its merits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current rotation and let the assistant sort notices after I checked them against the route sheet. I would keep the emergency fund at eleven months or better rather than spend it to follow a small trend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work and pay in this mild case. I would be glad if a useful screen saved time, as long as the person in the cab still had authority to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop using its notices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it missed a tire warning or a radio closure, I would pause and compare it with the signed route sheet. I would tell the mechanic and the next crew what detail had been left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell whether it had saved time without losing the important details?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a month of notices with the service log and count what the crew had to add back. If the warnings stayed complete, I would let it keep sorting the routine parts.

say: I would let a small tool sort notices, but **people make safety calls**.
I will keep **route checks** in the loop even if a screen saves time.
think: I think my hands-on job and pay stay **secure** in this scenario.
My eleven-month fund lets me **judge the tool calmly**.
do: Keep my **current rotation** and check notices against the route sheet.
Maintain an **eleven-month emergency fund** or better.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own job and pay in this mild case.
S0.quote: I will keep my own route checks in the loop, even if a screen saves time.
fieldNote: Amira accepts a small tool only when people retain **safety authority**.
Her **eleven-month reserve** and nearby employers make the mild case secure.
She proposes checking notices against **service logs** before expanding use.

steps.text: Keep the truck rotation and check notices against the route sheet
Wait one month of complete notices before expanding use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the planning tool is worth learning after another crew has proved it on our road. I would also ask the mine to tell us whether route checks or lead hours are changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my shift is still driving, but I do route checks and write handover notes as a lead. I am uneasy that those tasks could move to software and leave me with more checking work but less paid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would wait for another crew to test the planner, then compare its route with the mine's signed map. If it proved accurate, I would learn that feature on a paid shift and ask who remains responsible for a wrong route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because my own driving looks secure but the lead tasks could be reorganized. I would check the allowance and handover time on my pay slip instead of assuming every saved minute becomes a staff cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which change would tell you that the new software had affected your role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for fewer paid lead hours or more routes assigned without an operator's check. If I saw either, I would bring the rota to the foreman and ask for a paid retraining path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planner disagreed with the signed map, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stop the trial route and ask another experienced driver to inspect the road with me. If the system had missed a change in the ground, I would report it and keep the current route until it was corrected.

say: I would learn the planner after another crew **proves it** on our road.
I would ask whether lead hours or **route checks** are changing.
think: I think my driving work remains **mostly hands-on**.
I worry about more checking work and **less paid time**.
do: Wait for another crew to test the **route planner**.
Learn the feature on paid time and clarify **route responsibility**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because lead tasks may change while driving remains.
S1.quote: I would say the planning tool is worth learning after another crew has proved it on our road.
fieldNote: Amira waits for **peer proof** before adopting a new system.
Her concern is **unpaid review work**, not immediate loss of the truck.
She checks **pay and handover time** rather than assuming a staff cut.

steps.text: Wait for another crew to test the route planner on site
Learn the planner feature during a paid shift after it is proven

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain that thinking AI comes first and robots reach hands-on work about three years later. I would ask for funded courses and a real list of openings, because two years is too short for workers to plan from slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my haul-truck hours could shrink by 2031, even if the first change is to planning and records. Eleven months saved gives me a buffer, but I would still start looking at physical inspection work before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the mine to fund a physical equipment-inspection course and enroll if it did. In 2029, after AGI arrives, I would apply for an inspection post only if it involved hands-on checks and had a clear wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because robots could reduce my main paid task within five years, and that is close enough to plan around. My savings and nearby mines give me choices, but I do not know how many people will be hired for inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if inspection work is mostly records and planning, which AGI can already do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would not treat the job title as protection; AGI can do that thinking work. I would ask how much of the position is a physical check and how many paid posts remain after robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine cannot give a wage or duration for the post in 2029, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my truck job and compare openings at the other mines before spending on another course. I would apply only when the work and pay were written down, because I do not need to jump without a plan.

say: I would explain that robots follow thinking AI by **three years**.
I would ask for **funded courses** and actual openings.
think: I think my truck hours could shrink by **2031**.
Eleven months saved gives me a buffer, but I need to **plan early**.
do: Ask the mine to fund and enroll me in a **physical inspection course**.
In 2029, apply only for hands-on checks with a **clear wage**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because robots could reduce my main paid task within five years.
S2.quote: I think my haul-truck hours could shrink by 2031, even if the first change is to planning and records.
fieldNote: Amira sees a **specific earnings risk** by the robot date.
Her savings give her choices, but do not guarantee a **new vacancy**.
She distinguishes physical inspection from **records AGI can handle**.

steps.text: Enroll in the mine-funded physical equipment-inspection course
Apply for hands-on inspection work with a clear wage in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough time to train if the mine pays for it and publishes the job numbers. I will not call a physical job permanent when robots are due in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight years gives me time to learn how mechanics inspect the fleet while I keep my regular pay. The thinking records could go at AGI, so I would not count a desk role as a safe move after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would complete the mine's paid inspection course before 2031 and keep my truck qualification current. In 2032, the first year after AGI arrives, I would apply for physical inspection work only if the wage and expected duration were clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I have time to prepare, but no one knows how many physical jobs will remain after 2034. I would keep my current income while I trained instead of leaving for a short contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you pay for training beyond the mine's course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two nearby mines whether the credential qualifies workers for physical inspections and what graduates earn. If it only teaches record entry, I would not spend more money on it after AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the inspection post is only a bridge to 2034, what would you do in 2032?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take it if the pay covered my costs and gave me time to find the next role before robots arrived. If it did not, I would keep my truck shift and continue comparing openings.

say: I would say training needs pay and **published job numbers**.
I will not call physical work **permanent** when robots are due.
think: Eight years lets me learn while **keeping regular pay**.
I will not count a desk role as safe after **AGI**.
do: Complete the mine's **paid inspection course** before 2031 and keep my truck qualification current.
In 2032, apply only with clear **wage and duration**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because I can prepare, but later job numbers are unknown.
S3.quote: I will not call a physical job permanent when robots are due in 2034.
fieldNote: Amira views the longer lead as **time to train** while earning.
She rejects records work as a safe **fallback after AGI**.
She checks **graduate pay** and later vacancies before moving.

steps.text: Complete the mine's paid physical inspection course before 2031
Apply for physical inspection work with stated pay in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the ten-year lead gives us time to plan, but the mine should share actual training routes and vacancies. I would not tell people to leave a good job just because the date is on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have time to make a careful move, and no reason to leave a good wage early. I would explore physical inspection training, but I would check whether that work still exists after robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current rotation and review which paid courses have led to jobs at nearby mines. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrives, I would compare physical vacancies and pay before deciding whether to transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because my income and savings give me time to plan around the later robot date. I would stay where I am until a new job had clear physical duties and a wage worth changing for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What information would you need before changing mines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the job is physical, what it pays and how long the employer expects to keep the post. I would also check whether the training credential works at more than one mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the vacancy information is still unclear in 2037, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the truck job while asking the other mines for current figures. I would wait to transfer until a real vacancy and wage were in writing.

say: I would ask for **training routes and vacancies** before deciding.
I would not leave a good job just because **a date is stated**.
think: I have time for a careful move while **my present job pays**.
I will check if physical inspection lasts after **2039**.
do: Review **paid courses** and their graduate employers at nearby mines.
In 2037, compare physical vacancies and **pay** before transferring to another mine.
feel: I feel **calm** because my income and savings give me time.
S4.quote: I have time to make a careful move, and no reason to leave a good wage early.
fieldNote: Amira treats the decade as **time to plan**, not a reason to quit.
Her income and savings support a **deliberate choice**.
She checks whether physical training transfers across **multiple mines**.

steps.text: Keep the current truck rotation while reviewing paid course outcomes
Wait for a written physical vacancy and wage before transferring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could affect my main work by about 2031. Paid training, reliable job numbers and enough time to check wages would help me make a move without rushing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I want the person on the road to be able to question the machine's answer. A tool can help us notice a problem, but workers still need the right to stop when the ground disagrees.

headlineQuote: I want the person on the road to be able to question the machine's answer.
portrait: Amira Larsen is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
She earns **higher pay** and has eleven months of expenses saved.
Plenty of nearby mines give her **options** if her role changes.
She uses AI occasionally and confirms unfamiliar **technical wording** with a mechanic.
She is open to proven tools but will not assume physical jobs last after **robots**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives only about five years before robots could reduce her truck work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, reliable vacancy numbers and time to compare wages would help Amira plan a move.
